messages.author: a08a2def4527ebe2
messages.subject: Prior for orderd vector
parts:
Hi everyone, 

a very brief question: what is the default prior for an ordered vector? 

Is it a flat prior (i.e. U(-inf,inf)) for the first element, and thereafter x_n~U(x_(n-1),inf) for the rest?

I found the discussion of Jacobians in chapter 58 in the manual, but couldn't see the default prior spelled out explicitly anywhere (except a general discussion on page 53).

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Prior for orderd vector
parts:
On Monday, November 7, 2016 at 2:26:51 AM UTC-5, Ole Petter Hansen wrote:
a very brief question: what is the default prior for an ordered vector? 

Is it a flat prior (i.e. U(-inf,inf)) for the first element, and thereafter x_n~U(x_(n-1),inf) for the rest?

Not really, because all elements but the last are going to have a random upper bound too. I would simply say that all vectors satisfying the constraints are equally likely before seeing the data. I don't even really like the phrase "default prior". You define a space by declaring what the parameter type is (and its lower and upper bounds, which can be infinite). And then in the model block you can describe the shape of your beliefs over that space with an explicit prior. If you don't, then you are simply left with that space until you condition on the data.

Ben

messages.author: a08a2def4527ebe2
messages.subject: Re: Prior for orderd vector
parts:
Won't that depend on what we are conditioning on? I.e. x_n can take all values from x_(n-1) to infty before conditioning on x_(n+1). This seems to be the logic in section 58.5 in the manual, where the unconstrained transforms of an ordered vector are defined recursively. So it is at least not apparent to me that the last element of the vector is treated any differently than anyone in the middle (unless we are interested in the distribution of x_n | x_(n-1), x_(n+1) ). 

So just to clarify: If I would like to have an ordered vector where each element is defined recursively with support x_n~U(x_(n-1),infty), then I would have to define this myself using e.g. transformed parameters?

E.g. if I want an ordered vector x of length 3, I should do this as follows: 

parameters{
real x_first_element;
real[2] x_inc;
}

transformed parameters{
vector[3] x;

x[1]=x_first_element[1];
x[2]=x_inc[1]+x[1];
x[3]+x_inc[2]+x[2];
}

Do I understand you correctly that defining ordered[3] x; directly would imply a different prior?

Thank you for your response. 

Ole-Petter

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Prior for orderd vector
parts:
On Monday, November 7, 2016 at 1:13:06 PM UTC-5, Ole Petter Hansen wrote:
E.g. if I want an ordered vector x of length 3, I should do this as follows: 

parameters{
real x_first_element;
real[2] x_inc;
}

This would need to be

real<lower=0> x_inc[2];

}

Do I understand you correctly that defining ordered[3] x; directly would imply a different prior?

In this case, the Jacobian determinant of the transformation from {x_first, x_inc[1], x_inc[2]} to {x[1], x[2], x[3]} is 1, so this would be equivalent to declaring ordered[3] x in the parameters block. Maybe I misunderstood what you were saying before.

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Prior for orderd vector
parts:
All of Stan's parameters work the same way. The distribution
is uniform over all values satisfying the constraint. If you
want to see how we do that, there's a chapter near the end of
the manual on the Jacobians for constrained parameters.

The uniformity assumption means that if you add your own prior
for a variable, that's the prior it has because the uniform doesn't
add anything (a log constant, which can be ignored in all of our
algorithms).

- Bob
